messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mariam was a 36-year-old Middle Eastern woman who had built her life around hard physical work, long shifts on construction sites, and the steady routines of a marriage that had otherwise felt dependable. The trouble began after a sudden, life-threatening illness that struck without warning and left her frightened by how close she had come to dying. One evening she was at home when she became acutely ill, her body failing in a way that felt immediate and unfamiliar, and she remembers the panic of not being able to trust what was happening inside her. After that, ordinary sensations took on a dangerous meaning. If her heart beat a little faster on the job, or if her body felt unusual, she became jumpy and easily startled, as though danger might be about to break in again. At night she lay in bed tense and braced, unable to settle, sometimes taking a long time to fall asleep and sometimes waking repeatedly, her body feeling as though it were still waiting for the next collapse. At work she noticed herself scanning for anything that might signal trouble, but that watchfulness only made her feel more wound up and unable to relax.

In the weeks that followed, Mariam came to believe that her reactions meant something was badly wrong with her mind. She was certain that the intensity of her fear and the way she stayed keyed up must mean she was going crazy, and that belief made the experience even more alarming. She also became convinced that she had no future worth imagining, because if her own body had turned against her once, she felt helpless to stop bad things from happening again. Those thoughts made it harder for her to tolerate being still with herself, and she began pushing the feelings away rather than sitting with them. When the memories or the bodily tension rose up, she threw herself into work or kept adding tasks around the house so she would not have to think. After exhausting shifts, she would eat more than usual in the evenings, not because she was hungry but because the food gave her something immediate and dulling to focus on. She described it as a way to distract herself or feel better for a little while. At other times she emotionally numbed herself, trying not to feel anything at all, as though if she stayed blank enough she might not have to face what had happened.

But the more she relied on those strategies, the more they seemed to confirm the frightening story she had built about herself. When she noticed that she was overeating, overworking, or going emotionally flat, she took it as further evidence that she was losing control. Each episode fed her fear that her reactions meant she was going crazy, and her hopelessness deepened because she could not see a way back to feeling like herself. Her sense of helplessness also intensified: if she could not stop the distress, she concluded, then she could not stop the next disaster either. That made the body-on-alert feeling even more persistent, and the cycle became harder to interrupt. Some nights she would leave work so drained that she ate standing over the kitchen counter without tasting the food, then went to bed with her muscles still tight, listening for her own heartbeat and waiting for sleep that would not come.

At the construction site, this cycle had begun to affect her functioning in concrete ways. Mariam still showed up and kept working, but she often overextended herself, taking on tasks past the point of fatigue because staying busy felt safer than thinking. She told herself that if she kept moving, she could outrun the fear. Instead, she became more exhausted and more irritable, and her marriage had started to absorb some of the strain, with her husband noticing how distant and shut down she had become in the evenings. Even when she tried to rest, her body stayed tense, and a sudden clang of metal or a shouted instruction on site could make her jump hard enough that coworkers noticed.

By the time she sought help, Mariam was worn down by the combination of sleeplessness, constant tension, and the conviction that she was not thinking or reacting normally. What finally brought her in was the fear that this pattern was becoming her whole life: work, food, and numbness on one side, panic and dread on the other. She hoped for relief from the feeling that her body was always on the edge of danger, but what frightened her most was the possibility that her mind had been permanently damaged by the illness and that she would never be able to trust herself again.
